Full text

Abstract

Africa played a key role in the ALLS data collection, which would not have been possible without their dedicated efforts, especially their direct engagement with participants throughout the process. We would therefore like to thank all those who contributed to this data collection.

We have no conflicts of interest to report.

[div-01]

Research goal: Personality traits describe how we think, feel, and behave. More agentic people, for example, tend to be more confident, sociable, and fearless, whereas more communal people are more respectful, moral, warm, and even-tempered. Research has shown that personality traits such as agency and communion predict life outcomes such as health, well-being, and employment. However, the evidence for this comes almost exclusively from Western countries. We tested whether the links between personality traits and important life outcomes replicate in African contexts and whether these links are robust across different ways to analyze the data.

Methods: Using a sample of young adults from Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,770), we examined how personality traits are related to life outcomes like health, employment, and depression over 2 to 3 years.

Findings:

We found that more agentic and more communal people tended to have higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression. Being more communal also predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later. However, the associations were smaller than in Western countries and depended on factors such as the time lag between assessments. Our findings provide important insights into how links between personality traits and life outcomes differ across cultural contexts.

Personality Predictors of Health, Well-Being, Relationships, and Employment in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study

Personality traits -characteristic patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors -have been found to predict outcomes across important life domains, including educational attainment (Mammadov, 2022; Noftle & Robins, 2007), relationship success (Wagner et al., 2015), income (Denissen et al., 2018), health (Jokela et al., 2018; Kern & Friedman, 2011), the occurrence of major life stressors (Santee et al., 2023), and mortality (Jokela et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2007).

The predictive power of personality traits seems to be on par with or even to surpass that of other commonly-studied predictors like socio-economic status or cognitive abilities (Roberts et al., 2007). Furthermore, personality-outcome links have been replicated across samples, a range of possible covariates, and research methods (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023), underlining the robustness of personality-outcome associations (Bleidorn et al., 2019).

Findings on the predictive power of personality traits, however, stem almost exclusively from Western countries, home to only 11% of the world's population (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, 2024). For example, a systematic review by Roberts et al. (2007) included only one study conducted in Asia and not a single one from South America or Africa. A later mega-analysis by Beck and Jackson (2022) included only datasets collected in Western countries. Although a handful of studies have tested personality-outcome associations in African countries, these were typically limited by small samples, non-validated personality inventories, and/or cross-sectional designs (Du Preez et al., 2011; Kinyanjui & Sum, 2023; Nel et al., 2017; Papenfus et al., 2024; Peltzer, 2002). These limitations leave unclear whether findings on personality-outcome associations generalize to African countries. As virtually all psychological phenomena are impacted by cultural context, it cannot be assumed that findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries generalize to all people (Henrich et al., 2010; Kitayama & Salvador, 2024).

With the present study, we address the cross-cultural generalizability of personalityoutcome links. To do so, we use longitudinal data from the Africa Long Life Study (Thalmayer et al., 2024), which, as of 2025, had assessed personality traits and life outcomes over 3 years among young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. We examine longitudinal associations between personality traits and seven important life outcomes: self-reported health, subjective well-being, depression, anxiety, relationship status, employment status, and subjective financial status. Furthermore, we use specification curve analyses to investigate the robustness of these associations across various analytic decisions such as covariates or country.

Empirical Evidence on Personality-Outcome Associations

Over the last decades, robust predictive links between personality traits and various important life outcomes have been identified, highlighting the practical and societal relevance of personality traits (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Bleidorn et al., 2019; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). Most studies on this topic focused on the Big Five personality traitsagreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, emotional stability, and opennessand examined outcomes across life domains such as well-being, health, work, and relationships (Bleidorn, 2024; Bleidorn et al., 2019). Table 1 provides an overview of the existing evidence on personality-outcome associations, focusing on large-scale longitudinal studies and metaanalyses. For example, there is consistent evidence that higher levels of conscientiousness and extraversion predict better health status several years later, whereas higher levels of neuroticism have consistently been linked to mental health problems like depression and anxiety (Kotov et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2022; Turiano et al., 2012; Wright & Jackson, 2023). The size of personality-outcome links differs across outcomes and studies, but most studies found at least medium-sized associations of r = .20 (Funder & Ozer, 2019; Roberts et al., 2007).

These findings appear to provide a solid knowledge basis regarding the predictive power of personality traits. However, it is unclear whether these personality-outcome associations can be replicated in non-Western countries. Investigating these effects in sub-Saharan Africa is of importance because this region provides a meaningful cultural contrast to Western contexts in various socio-cultural and ecological respects, making for a compelling test of cross-cultural replicability of current theories. It is also home to more of the world's population than all Western countries combined (United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division, 2024), making the predictive utility of personality trait measures an important practical question.

There are several reasons to anticipate that findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries might not generalize to sub-Saharan Africa. First, the most important personality traits and their structure differ in African compared to Western societies (Thalmayer et al., 2020 (Thalmayer et al., , 2021)). While most research in Western countries has focused on the Big Five personality traits (Bleidorn, 2024), it has recently been shown that the Big Two personality traits, agency and communion, may work better for cross-cultural comparisons in personality research (Thalmayer et al., 2025). Agency describes the tendency to be confident, sociable, fearless, surgent, and positive, akin to the Big Five traits extraversion, openness, and low negative emotions (emotional stability). Communion describes the tendency to be warm, respectful, moral, diligent, and even-tempered, akin to the Big Five traits agreeableness, conscientiousness, and even-temper (emotional stability).

Second, cultural contexts differ in what kind of behaviors are considered appropriate or desirable, and thus are rewarded or punished, which likely influences personality-outcome associations (Hofstede, 2011; Leung & Cohen, 2011). Relatedly, individuals living in low-andmiddle-income countries, including those in sub-Saharan Africa, are faced with a greater degree of contextual challenges, including social, economic, and political risks (Herrero Romero et al., 2018; Uskul et al., 2024), making them more likely to experience poverty, crime, and domestic violence (Gradín, 2019; Theron et al., 2022). These challenging conditions may influence the kind of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that are adaptive and thus influence personalityoutcome associations.

Third, there is evidence that young adults living in sub-Saharan Africa report different kinds of life events and differ in their personality-event transactions compared to young adults from Western countries, indicating that the interplay between personality traits and the environment may differ across cultural contexts (Haehner et al., 2026).

In sum, although there is robust evidence on personality-outcome associations in Western societies, it is unclear whether these findings generalize to sub-Saharan Africa. Only a few small and cross-sectional studies have linked personality traits to life outcomes such as mental health, well-being, and health behaviors in African samples (Du Preez et al., 2011; Kinyanjui & Sum, 2023; Papenfus et al., 2024; Peltzer, 2002). For example, Nel et al. (2017) found medium to strong associations between well-being and conscientiousness (β = 0.19), emotional stability (β = 0.55), and extraversion (β = 0.26) in young adults from South Africa.

One previous study provided initial insights into longitudinal personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa using data from the Africa Long Life Study (Kura et al., 2025). This study investigated whether markers of HEXACO/Big Six personality traits were related to mental and physical health. The authors found, for example, that higher levels of conscientiousness and openness predicted better self-reported health 2 years later. However, this study did not examine outcomes from other life domains and did not use thein this cultural contextmore psychometrically-sound Cross-Cultural Big Two personality traits. Furthermore, findings on personality-outcome associations differed across countries and assessment waves, highlighting the necessity to test their robustness. It is thus a first goal of the present study to examine longitudinal personality-outcome associations in three sub-Saharan countries and to compare results to those from Western countries.

Examining the Robustness of Personality-Outcome Associations

Although personality-outcome links have been replicated across samples and research methods in Western countries, their robustness in non-Western countries has yet to be established (Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019). Only if personality-outcome links are robust, will they have practical relevance in the region, for example, in appropriately informing public health interventions (Bleidorn et al., 2019; Haehner, Wright, et al., 2024; Wright et al., 2026).

However, several analytic decisions, like the covariates included or the time interval between assessments, can influence the results on personality-outcome associations. For instance, Beck and Jackson (2022) have shown that the predictive link between conscientiousness and employment status depends on age.

Thus, the second goal of the present study is to examine the robustness of personalityoutcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa. To do so, we use specification curve analysis as a pragmatic way to test the relevance of different analytic decisions and to integrate a large number of results (similar to the approach of Beck & Jackson, 2022). With specification curve analysis, researchers first identify and estimate all reasonable ways to specify a statistical model (Simonsohn et al., 2020). In our case, we test the robustness of personality-outcome associations across different covariates, countries, and ways of capturing personality trait scores. We then conduct a joint statistical test to examine whether all possible specifications support or refute a significant personality-outcome association.

The Present Study

The present study tests longitudinal personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa. To do so, we use data from the Africa Long Life Study (ALLS; Thalmayer et al., 2024), which has assessed personality traits and important life outcomes such as employment status, self-reported health, and subjective well-being in young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa since 2022, providing up to 3 years of data at this time. Using these data, we address two research questions: (1) Which personality traits are associated with important life outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa and how do effect sizes compare to results from Western countries? (2) How robust are personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa and which analytic decisions influence effect sizes?

As evidence on personality-outcome associations from sub-Saharan Africa is still limited, we relied mainly on findings from Western countries to derive hypotheses. Based on the existing evidence on personality-outcome associations (see Table 1) and the conceptual overlap of the Big Two and Big Five taxonomies, we developed nine hypotheses for the present study (Table 2). These hypotheses may be seen as a useful starting point for a more thorough empirical investigation of personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa as they provide benchmarks for comparisons. However, as described above, there are also several reasons why findings from Western countries might not generalize to Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Thus, deviations from these hypotheses should not be interpreted as contradicting prior empirical evidence but rather as indications of potential cultural differences, underlining the necessity of cross-cultural research.

Methods

Transparency and Openness

ALLS data collection strategies and measures were approved by each of the five partner universities [BLINDED FOR REVIEW] and at the national levels in Kenya and Namibia, as well as the county level in Kenya. Data from ALLS have been used in 11 previous publications and preprints [BLINDED FOR REVIEW]. One of these studies reported longitudinal associations between personality traits and health. However, no study tested the robustness of a broad range of personality-outcome associations. Furthermore, personality trait data from Wave 7 has not been analyzed before. Data, analysis scripts, a codebook, and an HTML document with Supplementary Materials can be retrieved from https://osf.io/4uz5s/?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7. The hypotheses and analyses were preregistered at https://osf.io/5zw4a/?view_only=8fc2fe2a1fd74397889c3873e8d5f412. Deviations from the preregistration are described in https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7. We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

Procedure

ALLS is an ongoing longitudinal study with assessment waves every 6 months. For this study, we used data from Waves 1, 3, and 7 (henceforward called W1, W3, and W7), collected between 2022 and 2025. ALLS participants are young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, mainly aged 18, but up to age 21, at W1. They were recruited by local research assistants who found eligible individuals at schools, church groups, and community events. To compensate for dropout, booster samples were added at W3 using the same data collection methods.

To take part in the study, participants provided written informed consent, then they completed the first survey either on an electronic tablet carried by a research assistant, on paper, or via a link sent to participant's device. Each wave comprised questionnaires about personality traits, well-being, mental health, cultural mindset, and socio-demographic characteristics. All surveys were in English. Participants were recontacted for subsequent waves either online or in-person via local research assistants, which allowed for a more representative sample compared to an online-only study in these contexts. More details about the design and measures of ALLS used can be found in Thalmayer and colleagues (2024).

Sample

At W1, 3,048 young adults were recruited to participate in ALLS. At W2, approximately 700 participants dropped out of the study or could not be reached again so a booster sample of 723 participants was added at W3. For the present analyses, we restricted the sample to participants who took part in W7 and in either W1 or W3. Furthermore, we excluded participants who failed to pass attention check items (e.g., "Which of the following is a building?", with response options house, tree, plane, cat, and book). Applying these exclusion criteria led to a final sample of N = 2,770. With this sample size, we had a sufficient power of 80% to detect very small personality-outcome associations of r = .053 (Champely, 2006; Funder & Ozer, 2019).

At W1, 55% of the sample identified as female. Participants were, on average, 18.32 years old (SD = 0.76), with 58% reporting having completed high school and 36% reported to be looking for employment. Further sample characteristics can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7.

Measures

Personality Traits (W1 and W3)

The Big Two personality traits agency and communion were assessed with the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory (Thalmayer et al., 2025). The 45 Items (e.g., "I tend to be calm") were rated on a 6-point response scale ranging from 1 (very inaccurate) to 6 (very accurate).

After reverse scoring items, as necessary, we calculated mean scores. The Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory was found to assess personality traits reliably in the present sample (.79 ≤ α ≤ .90) and to fulfill the criteria of (partial) strong measurement invariance across Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (Haehner et al., 2026; Thalmayer et al., 2025).

Self-Reported Health (W7)

Self-reported health was assessed with a single item ("In general, would you say your health is...") rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent).

Life Satisfaction (W7)

Life satisfaction was assessed with the three-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; Kjell & Diener, 2021). Items (e.g., "I am satisfied with my life") were rated on a 7-point response scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). We calculated mean scores (α = .80).

Depression and Anxiety (W7)

Depression and anxiety were assessed with the relevant subscales of the International Mental Health Assessment (Thalmayer et al., 2023). The 16 items of these subscales (e.g., "I felt scared") were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from 0 (not in the last month/never) to 6 (daily). We calculated mean scores for the analyses (anxiety: α = .85, depression: α = .87).

Relationship Status (W7)

Relationship status was assessed with a single item "Are you in a romantic relationship?" with five response options:0 = I am not in a relationship,1 = I am in a relationship but do not live with my partner,2 = I am in a relationship and live with my partner,

To increase power and facilitate the analyses, we collapsed this into two groups:0 = not in a relationship (former Option 0) and1 = in a relationship (former Options 1 to 3).

Employment Status (W7)

Employment status was assessed with a single item "Which best describes your current work situation?" with six response options:0 = unemployed,1 = full time learner/student,2 = studying and working,3 = occasional paid work,4 = regular part-time paid work,5 = regular full-time paid work. To increase power and facilitate the analyses, we collapsed this into two groups:0 = unemployed (former Option 0) and1 = employed/in education (former Options 1 to 5).

Subjective Financial Situation (W7)

Subjective financial situation was assessed with a single item "How would you describe the financial situation of your household?" rated with three response options:1 = we have great difficulties, our financial situation is bad,2 = sometimes we have slight difficulties, but our situation is average, and3 = we do not have any financial problems, our financial situation is good. We recoded subjective financial situation into two categories:0 = bad (former Option 1) and1 = average or good (former Options 2 and 3).

Family Affluence (W1)

We used six items (e.g., "Do you have your own bedroom for yourself") from the Family Affluence Scale II (Boyce et al., 2006; Rotzinger et al., 2024) to assess family affluence. Item responses (0 = no,1 = yes) were summed across items.

Data Analyses

Data analyses were conducted in R (Version 4.3.2) using R packages specr (Masur & Scharkow, 2020) and lavaan (Rosseel, 2012). We used a level of α = .05 for all analyses and standardized all metric variables. Our analyses comprised two parts. First, we examined personality-outcome associations using longitudinal correlations to obtain effect size estimates that can be compared to findings from Western countries. Then, we used specification curve analyses to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations across different analytic decisions.

Research Question 1: Longitudinal Correlations

We calculated longitudinal correlations between personality traits assessed at W1 (n = 1,720 for agency and n = 1,714 for communion) and life outcomes assessed at W7.

If W1 personality data was not available, we used W3 personality trait scores (n = 572 for agency and n = 578 for communion). We used Pearson correlations for metric life outcomes (e.g., life satisfaction) and point-biserial correlations for binary life outcomes (e.g., employment status).

We focused on the size of correlations and compared these effect sizes to findings from Western countries (see Table 1).

Research Question 2: Specification Curve Analysis

Specification curve analysis allowed us to examine the consistency of results across a broad range of possible model specifications. With specification curve analysis, all valid model specifications are first estimated, and then the robustness of effects across these specifications is tested systematically (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

We estimated one specification curve for each trait-outcome combination (i.e., 14 specification curves in total). Life outcomes assessed at W7 served as dependent variables.

Personality traits assessed at W1 or W3 served as predictors. We either used linear or logistic regression models for the specification curve analyses, depending on whether the dependent variable was metric or binary. Specification curve analyses comprised three steps.

Step 1: Identification of All Specifications of Interest.

As a first step, we identified all reasonable ways to specify our regression models. In our case, we estimated models with different covariates, (sub)samples, ways to calculate personality trait scores, and retest intervals. In total, we examined 256 model specifications for each trait-outcome combination.

Analytic Decision 1: Covariates.

Demographic characteristics like age, gender, family affluence, and education may confound the association between personality traits and important life outcomes. Similar to Beck and Jackson (2022), we examined whether personality-outcome relations were robust across models with different covariates.

Analytic Decision 2: Sample.

ALLS comprises individuals living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Personality-outcome relations might differ across the three ALLS countries (Kura et al., 2025). We thus tested the consistency of personality-outcome associations across the three subsamples and in the overall sample.

Analytic Decision 3: Different Ways to Estimate Personality Trait Scores.

In prior research, personality-outcome associations have typically been examined using manifest variables (e.g., Beck & Jackson, 2022; Soto, 2019; Wright & Jackson, 2023). However, latent variables help to account for measurement error. We thus tested the consistency of personalityoutcome associations between manifest and latent trait score calculations. To create latent personality trait scores, we used the predicted factor scores from unidimensional structural equation models as by Haehner et al. (2026). Haehner et al. (2026) tested different measurement models of the Cross-Cultural Big Two Inventory against each other by comparing models with and without removing certain items. Here, we relied on the measurement models including all items to increase comparability with manifest scores even though they had mediocre fit (Agency W1: CFI = .81, RMSEA = .09, Communion W1: CFI = .90, RMSEA = .09). These models were estimated using the indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood estimation. More details about latent measurement models including correlations between latent and manifest personality trait scores can be found in Section 1 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7.

Analytic Decision 4: The Retest Interval.

We either used W1 or W3 personality data to examine personality-outcome associations. W1 personality data allowed us to examine a longer retest interval (i.e., 3 years), whereas W3 personality data led to a larger sample size.

Step 2: Descriptive Specification Curve.

In the second step, we estimated all possible model specifications identified in Step 1. We then depicted the result in a descriptive specification curve, which illustrates the effect size of interest -ranked from lowest/most negative to highest/most positive -along with the corresponding model specifications. For metric outcomes, we focused on standardized regression coefficients. For binary outcomes, we used odds ratios. Furthermore, we examined and visualized which analytic decisions mattered the most for the effect size of interest.

Step 3: Joint Statistical Tests.

In the third step, we calculated joint statistical tests to examine whether the full set of specifications counters the null hypothesis that there is no association between the predictor and the outcome variable (Simonsohn et al., 2020). For these joint statistical tests, we used the permutation-test technique similar to the procedures of Beck and Jackson (2022), Haehner et al. (2024), and Rohrer (2017). With the permutation-test technique, we first created a dataset under the null hypothesis (i.e., no association). We used two different approaches to achieve this goal: We either shuffled the values of personality traits across participants or we shuffled the values of life outcomes across participants. In these datasets, we estimated all model specifications. We then repeated the previous two steps 500 times to generate a distribution of specification curves under the null hypotheses. Finally, we used this distribution to conduct two statistical tests (Simonsohn et al., 2020). First, we estimated the median effect size in each specification curve under the null and compared it to the observed https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 specification curve of the original sample. Second, we computed the average p value in each specification curve under the null (transformed to z values using Stouffer's method) and compared it with the average observed p value in the specification curve of the original sample.

Results

Descriptive statistics of all study variables are summarized in Table 3. Further descriptive statistics and supplementary analyses can be found in the HTML document with https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 accompanying this manuscript.

Research Question 1: Longitudinal Correlations

Longitudinal personality-outcome correlations assessed over 2 to 3 years are illustrated in Figure 1. As can be seen in this figure, higher levels of agency predicted higher levels of life satisfaction (r = .05, 95% CI = [.00, .09]) and self-rated health (r = .07, 95% CI = [.03, .11]), lower levels of anxiety (r = -.08, 95% CI = [-.12, -.04]) and depression (r = -.11, 95% CI = [-.15, -.07]), being in a relationship (r = .04, 95% CI = [.00, .09]), and being employed (r = .05, 95% CI = [.01, .09]) 2 to 3 years later. Similarly, higher levels of communion predicted higher levels of life satisfaction (r = .05, 95% CI = [.00, .09]), lower levels of anxiety (r = -.06.95% CI = [-.10, -.02]), and being employed (r = .06, 95% CI = [.02, .10]) 2 to 3 years later. Although these correlations were statistically significant, they were small according to common effectsize guidelines (Funder & Ozer, 2019).

Research Question 2: Specification Curve Analyses

Next, we estimated specification curves to examine the robustness of personalityoutcome associations across different analytic decisions. Specifically, we tested whether personality-outcome associations were robust across different covariates, time intervals between assessments, countries, and ways to calculate personality trait scores, leading to 256 model specifications for each personality-outcome association.

Figure 2 illustrates the specification curve for one personality-outcome association (see Section 3 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 for all other specification curves). This specification curve shows how the predictive link between agency and self-rated health varied across model specifications. About half of the 256 models showed a positive and statistically-significant association between agency and self-rated health. Country and the way personality was scored seemed to be the most influential analytic decisions, with stronger personality-health links in South Africa and Kenya and for manifest scores of agency. A similar pattern also emerged for other personality-outcome combinations.

Figure 3 illustrates how much of the observed differences in personality-outcome associations could be explained by certain analytic decisions. As can be seen in this figure, effect sizes of personality-outcome associations depended the most on the country of data collection and on whether personality traits were calculated as manifest or latent variables whereas the covariates (e.g., age, gender, education, family affluence) explained little variance in personality-outcome associationsfoot_0 . Across personality-outcome links, associations tended to be weaker for latent personality scores than for manifest scores and for longer time lags between assessments. In contrast, there was no clear pattern of how the country of data collection was related to effect size estimates. For example, agency-health links were strongest in Kenya while agency-life-satisfaction links were strongest in South Africa (see Section 3 of https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7

Materials for further details).

To test whether the whole set of specifications counters the null hypothesis that there is no association between a personality trait and a life outcome, we ran four different kinds of permutation tests (see Methods section for details). If all four tests were statistically significant, we interpreted the results as indicating a robust personality-outcome https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 decision rule to infer robustness). These permutation tests compare the observed result pattern across specifications (e.g., the median effect size of a personality-outcome association across all 256 specifications; βMedian) to 500 hypothetical scenarios where there should be no effect. The corresponding p values thus indicate whether the observed result pattern is more extreme than what would have been expected if there was no association. As summarized in Table 4, higher levels of agency were robustly linked to higher levels of selfrated health (βMedian = 0.05, p < .001), lower levels of anxiety (βMedian = -0.08, p < .001), and lower levels of depression (βMedian = -0.06, p < .001). Furthermore, higher levels of communion were robustly linked to higher levels of self-rated health (βMedian = 0.07, p < .001), lower levels of anxiety (βMedian = -0.04, p = .016), lower levels of depression (βMedian = -0.05, p < .001), and being employed (βMedian = 0.12, p < .001). As such, results were in line with Hypothesis 3 (agency and self-rated health), Hypothesis 4 (agency and depression), Hypothesis 5 (communion and depression), Hypothesis 6 (agency and anxiety), and Hypothesis 7 (communion and anxiety). However, we did not find robust evidence for Hypothesis 1 (agency and life satisfaction), Hypothesis 2 (communion and life satisfaction), Hypothesis 8 (communion and relationship status), or Hypothesis 9 (agency and employment status).

In a non-preregistered step, we additionally explored whether findings on employment status and subjective financial status depended on the scoring of these variables. For example, for employment status, we compared three scorings: unemployed vs. employed/education (main analyses), unemployed vs. employed, and unemployed vs. education. Replicating the results of our main analyses, communion was consistently related to not being unemployed but there were no robust links for other personality-outcome combinations (see Section 4 of https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7 for details).

Exploratory Analyses: Differences Among Big Two Components

Agency and communion are two broad personality traits that capture individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors at a relatively high level of aggregation.

According to Thalmayer et al. (2025), agency comprises lower-order components of competence, confidence, fearlessness, positive mood, sociability, and surgency, while communion comprises components of even-temper, industriousness, morality, respect, and warmth. In an exploratory analysis, we examined personality-outcome associations using these lower-order components instead of the manifest-latent distinction as the analytic decision (see Section 5 of the Supplementary Materials for details).

These analyses revealed some differences in personality-outcome associations among Big Two components, illustrating the value of examining associations at a finer-grained level (Figure 4).

For example, the agency-health link was primarily attributable to competence, fearlessness, positive mood, and surgency. Similarly, the link between employment status and communion seemed to depend on industriousness, morality, and warmth. Despite these differences, most of the personality-outcome associations identified as robust in our main analyses replicated with Big Two components as predictors. Components explained between 1% and 31% of the variance in effect size estimates, suggesting that differences between components are relevant for the size of personality-outcome associations but less important than country or time-lag differences.

Discussion

In the present study, we tested the cross-cultural generalizability of personality-outcome associations by examining longitudinal links between personality traits and seven important life outcomes in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa. Using specification curve analyses, we also tested the robustness of personality-outcome associations across analytic decisions (e.g., time lag between assessment, country of data collection). We found that higher levels of agency and communion consistently predicted higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression over 2 to 3 years. Additionally, higher levels of communion predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later. Although robust, the effect sizes of these personality-outcome associations were small (.02 ≤ |r| ≤ .11). Furthermore, some personality-outcome links that are well-established in Western countries, including personality predictors of life satisfaction and relationship status, did not replicate in our sub-Saharan samples. Differences among countries, lower-order components of the Big Two, and ways to score personality traits partially explained heterogeneity in personality-outcome associations. Here, we discuss similarities and differences between our findings and prior results from Western countries and explore possible reasons for the divergences.

Similarities in Personality-Outcome Associations Across Cultural Contexts

Our results partly replicated findings on personality-outcome associations from Western countries. In line with our hypotheses, which were based on those prior findings (see Table 2), higher levels of agency and communion were associated with better self-reported mental and physical health (Kotov et al., 2010; Soto, 2019; Turiano et al., 2012; Wright & Jackson, 2023).

Similar to personality-outcome associations in Western countries, these links were robust across a range of analytic decisions, such as different covariates (e.g., age, gender, education) and time lags between assessments (Beck & Jackson, 2022).

These similarities in personality-outcome associations across cultural contexts support the view that agency and communion may function as basic human traits, capturing "adaptive" characteristics across cultural contexts (Saucier et al., 2014). Agency (akin to high extraversion, high openness, and low negative emotions) reflects a general tendency to be confident, sociable, positive and competent. High levels of agency could lead to better mental and physical health through more active coping behaviors, greater stress resistance, and higher health literacy.

Communion (akin to high agreeableness, high conscientiousness, and being even-tempered) describes the tendency to be warm, moral, and diligent.

Higher levels of this trait could be linked to mental health through less risky behaviors, larger social support networks, and more consistent health behaviors (Friedman & Kern, 2014; Kern & Friedman, 2011).

Providing some nuance to these conclusions, exploratory analyses indicated that personality-outcome associations differed among lower-order components of the Big Two. For example, the link between employment status and communion was strongest for components of industriousness, morality, and warmth, suggesting that thoughts, feelings, and behaviors related to conscientiousness and agreeableness rather than emotional stability are most relevant for personality-work associations in sub-Saharan Africa. Consistent with results from Western countries, these findings illustrate the value of moving beyond broad trait domains to better understand personality-outcome links (Mõttus, 2016; Stewart et al., 2022).

Differences in Personality-Outcome Associations Across Cultural Contexts

Personality-outcome associations in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa also differed in some ways from Western findings. Perhaps the most striking difference was the overall lower level of personality-outcome associations, with zero-order correlations ranging from |r| = .02 to .11. These findings diverge from results of Haehner et al. (2026) who used the same sample but found larger selection effects for self-reported important life events than typically observed in Western countries. However, small associations between traits and mental health outcomes are in line with results by Kura and colleagues (2025) who also used the same sample but a different personality inventory. There are several possible reasons for the small associations between personality traits and life outcomes.

Methodological factors like ceiling effects and restricted variance could be at play.

Young adults in our sample rated their trait levels relatively highly, with average values of 4.5 on a scale from 1 to 6 and with less variance than typically seen in Western samples (De Vries et al., 2021; Haehner et al., 2022), potentially limiting their predictive utility. Methodological factors could also explain why associations differed between manifest and latent personality trait variables. Latent personality-outcome associations might have been smaller because latent they had less variance in our sample (see Section 1 of the https://osf.io/wczpj?view_only=6ca1f0349d7846509129ac6906b671c7). Relatedly, latent and manifest personality scores were only moderately correlated in this sample, indicating that observed variance in personality traits was only partly explained by underlying similarities among the items. This could be due to unreliability of the measure or problems with the measurement model, both of which could reduce personality-outcome associations. To test the relevance of these methodological factors, future research comparing findings across personality measures would be needed.

A substantive possibility is that contextual factors are functionally more important for predicting life outcomes in African contexts, limiting the predictive power of traits. Young adults in sub-Saharan Africa face interconnected societal challenges such as poverty, inequality, and high unemployment (Gradín, 2019; Theron et al., 2022). These challenges present structural barriers to achieving desired life outcomes, despite having high levels of agency and/or communion.

An indication supporting the relevance of contextual factors is the finding that country explained a large proportion of the effect size differences in specification curve analyses. Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa differ in ways that could help explain differences in personality-outcome associations. For example, the countries differ in youth unemployment rate (Kenya: 67%, South Africa: 46%, Namibia: 37%) and age of first marriage (Kenya: 25.6 years, Namibia: 29.2 years, South Africa: 31.0 years), potentially influencing personalityemployment and personality-relationship associations (Federation of Kenya Employers, 2024; South African Government, 2024; The World Bank, 2025; World Population Review, 2025). It was not the case, however, such that one country always showed the strongest or weakest associations. Thus, sampling differences are an alternative explanation for the country differences. The South African sample included more university students recruits, whereas almost all Namibian and Kenyan recruits were high school students at Wave 1. To tease these explanations apart, future research may need to replicate our findings in independent -and ideally representative -samples.

Differences in findings between our African samples and the West could also be related to the developmental period of emerging adulthood. In Western countries, emerging adulthood is often described as a life phase of exploration (Arnett, 2007; Roberts & Davis, 2016), whereas young adults in sub-Saharan Africa typically have strong aspirations (and pressures) for education and work to provide for their family and community (Naudé & Breshears, 2025; Rotzinger et al., 2025; Uugwanga et al., 2025). As such, adaptive personality traits and their associations with important life outcomes may differ more in this life phase, with personalityoutcome associations potentially being more similar during other life phases. Testing this explanation would require a replication of our study in different age groups.

Finally, there is initial evidence that personality traits are functionally different in sub-Saharan Africa compared to Western countries. For example, personality traits have been found to be less stable in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa than in Western countries (Haehner et al., 2026).

Furthermore, there seem to be cross-cultural differences in how people describe other individuals, with more collectivistic cultures outside the West favoring context-based over dispositional, trait-like descriptions (Church, 2009; Valchev et al., 2013). Similarly, personality traits are seen as more malleable and situation dependent in non-Western countries (Kanagawa et al., 2001). Personality traits may be a less salient topic for young adults in sub-Saharan Africa, used less frequently to describe themselves or others, and thus less relevant to explain individual differences in life outcomes (Thalmayer et al., 2022). If this is true, it may have far-reaching consequences for the cross-cultural applicability of personality theories. Personality traits might be a less meaningful (though certainly not meaningless) unit of study in sub-Saharan Africa, and contextually-embedded descriptions of persons may be more theoretically and practically useful.

In sum, several factors may account for differences in personality-outcome associations across cultural contexts ranging from methodological factors to functional differences in personality traits across cultural contexts. To tease apart the different explanations, future research on personality traits in sub-Saharan Africa is needed. Specifically, studies that examine personality-outcome links in different countries, across different life phases, and with multiple personality trait measures would be needed to better understand cross-cultural similarities and differences in the predictive effects of personality traits.

Limitations and Directions for Future Research

The present study has several limitations. First, personality traits and important life outcomes were assessed with self-report measures only. Self-reports may be prone to biases such as socially desirable responding or acquiescence, biasing the associations between personality traits and outcomes (Paulhus & Vazire, 2007). Furthermore, some life outcomes were only assessed with one or few items and analyzed in a dichotomized way, limiting their reliability, and potentially attenuating their effect sizes. Conversely, personality-outcome associations may have been inflated due to common-method variance. Future research using multi-method approaches, including peer reports of personality traits and objective and comprehensive assessments of important life outcomes could reduce the impact of these methodological factors.

Second, in the present study, we only examined correlational links between personality traits and important life outcomes. Identifying robust personality-outcome associations is a necessary first step to better understand the relevance of personality traits across cultural contexts. Future research testing the causality of these robust associations and identifying pathways mediating these effects is warranted, as the practical relevance of the present findings is contingent on the causality of effects. Studies examining within-person associations between personality traits and life outcomes could help to reach this goal (Grosz et al., 2024; Jokela et al., 2018; Rohrer, 2018; Stieger et al., 2021; Wright & Jackson, 2023). For such investigations, a high number of assessment waves are needed to provide reliable estimates of within-person effects. The continuing data collection of ALLS may allow such analyses in the future.

Third, the results of personality-outcome associations may depend on the time interval between assessments (Hopwood et al., 2022). We focused on the predictive effects over 2 to 3 years, but longer time intervals between assessments are needed to identify the long-term implications of personality traits. For example, it could be the case that the consequences of personality traits for relationships or employment require more time to unfold.

Fourth, we considered seven important life outcomes stemming from the health, work, and relationship domains. However, there are other important outcomes from these and other domains, such as health behaviors, relationship satisfaction, income, job satisfaction, or educational attainment, that we could not examine in the present study (e.g., Soto, 2019).

Relatedly, in the present study, we were not able to examine the mechanisms driving personality-outcome associations (i.e., how personality traits express in everyday life and how those momentary personality expressions lead to long-term outcomes). Future research is thus needed to gain a comprehensive understanding of personality-outcome associations in non-Western countries.

Fifth, for the specification curve analyses, we used the criterion that four of four statistical tests had to be significant to conclude that a personality-outcome link is robust.

However, as there are no established guidelines on how to interpret diverging results in specification curve analysis, this decision rule is somewhat arbitrary. A more liberal rule (e.g., three of four significant tests) would have resulted in an additional robust link between agency and relationship status. This again illustrates the relevance of analytic decision for findings and conclusions on personality-outcome associations.

Conclusion

The goals of the present study were to test the cross-cultural replicability of personalityoutcome associations and to probe the robustness of personality-outcome associations in sub-Saharan Africa. Using a large sample of young adults from Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa, we found that higher levels of agency and communion were linked to better self-reported health and lower levels of anxiety and depression. While these personality-outcome links were generally robust, specification curve analyses showed that effect sizes depended on country and different ways to capture personality traits. Interestingly, personality-outcome associations tended to be smaller in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa than in Western countries and some well-established personality-outcome links in Western countries (e.g., with life satisfaction or employment status) were not replicated. These differences may be explained by methodological factors (e.g., modeling choices) or functional differences of personality traits across cultural contexts, highlighting the necessity of future research on personality traits in sub-Saharan Africa. Furthermore, differences between personality-outcome associations at the level of lower-order components illustrate the value of more fine-grained personality-outcome examinations.
